lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Tiago (Mock Rodízio) | Lesson 4 -- Before It Becomes a Problem

listenings.text: Tiago, it's Walter, from the shop floor. Look, I don't want to make this bigger than it is, but the press has been running hot since Tuesday. We stop it, we let it cool, we start again. It's holding, more or less. The thing is, if it stops properly, we lose a day, maybe two, and the October slot is already tight. Maintenance says they can look at it, but not before next week. Anyway. I thought you should know. I have to go, they're waiting for me.

inference.title: The audio does not answer these. You do.
items: Walter says he does not want to make this bigger than it is. Why would he say that before telling you a problem?
He ends with "I have to go, they're waiting for me". What does that tell you about how much time he has to think about this?
If you do nothing today, who finds out first — and how?

post_skill.title: Talk about it
items: Walter told you, and asked for nothing. Is that useful or not?
Who in your factory tells you things like this — and who does not?
What would you need to know before you take this upstairs?
Have you ever been the person who said "more or less, it's holding"?

language_focus.title: Analyse and answer
items: Walter's message has two of these five. Which two — and which three are missing?
Line 2 says there's a risk that, not it will happen. Why does that matter to the person listening?
Line 3 gives a condition. What does it let the other person do that lines 1 and 2 do not?
If you delete line 5, what does your boss do with the message?

language_focus.title: Reveal answer key
list: Walter has 1 and 2 — the warning and the risk. Missing: the condition (3), the impact in numbers (4) and the request with a deadline (5).
A risk can still be avoided; a fact cannot. Saying it will stop when it has not stopped costs you credibility the day it holds.
The condition names the thing that would change the outcome — it turns a warning into a decision someone can make.
Nothing. Without a deadline it is news, and news goes to the bottom of the pile.
language_focus.note: Do not hand over the four parts as a rule before he finds them. Ask, wait, then open.

practice_a.text: Now take a real risk in your factory this week — something that has not gone wrong yet. Say the whole warning out loud: the heads-up, the risk, the condition, and the decision you need, with a date.

practice_b.title: Reveal answer key
list: There's a risk that the press stops before the end of the month.
The impact would be about four days on the customer's side.
Unless we get maintenance in before Friday, it will stop.
I need a decision by Wednesday morning.
Heads-up: the press has been running hot since Tuesday.
practice_b.note: Accept justified variations, on one condition: it has to contain a number or a date. A warning without either is not a warning.

items: Case 1 — the press
Walter's message, and it is now your problem. Maintenance cannot come before next week. The older press in building two could take part of the load, slowly.
Case 2 — the new supplier
The supplier you recommended last month has not confirmed the tooling date. It is nine days until the order has to go in. They answer the phone, but not the question.
Case 3 — your own team
Two of your four operators are on holiday in the same week in October. You approved both, separately, and only saw it today.
Case 4 — the audit
The March audit may ask for the certificate of every supplier in the chain. One of yours does not have it. There is time, but only if someone starts now.

production.title: Give the warning
items: Take Case 1. Give the whole warning out loud, without stopping: heads-up, risk, condition, decision needed — with a date.
Now Case 2. Who do you warn first, and what do you ask them for?
Case 3 is the one where the risk is your own mistake. What is your first sentence — and what do you NOT say first?
In Case 4 nothing is wrong yet and nothing will be, for months. How do you make someone care today?
Which of the four would you put in writing instead of saying out loud? Defend it.

discussion.title: Discussion
items: Is there such a thing as raising a risk too early?
Have you ever seen someone punished for warning people early? What happened?
Walter told you and asked for nothing. Is that his job, or yours?
In Brazil, is bad news at work said directly or wrapped up? Is it different with an American customer?
What does your boss do with a warning that has no number in it?
If you had to teach one person in your team to warn better, who would it be — and what would you tell them?

wrapup.title: Before you go
items: Say the four parts of a useful warning, in order.
Which of the four do you usually forget?
Name one risk in your factory right now that nobody has flagged. Who needs to hear it, and by when?
